title: AI Agents Are Not Employees Yet
thesis: AI agents are improving fast, but real adoption depends on reliability, cost, and safe failure rather than benchmark hype.
audience_action: Swipe away with a sharper test for agent claims: can it fail safely and consistently?

slides.headline: Would you hire a 1-in-3 failure?
slides.body: Agents are getting scary good. But reliability is still the part everyone tries to skip.
slides.footer: Swipe before you buy the hype

slides.headline: Agents jumped from 12% to 66%.
slides.body: OSWorld jumped from about 12% to 66.3%. Huge progress. Still about one failure in three.

slides.headline: The leaderboard is lying by omission.
slides.body: One score hides cost, consistency, predictability, and how bad failure gets.
slides.footer: A score is not a product

slides.headline: Reliability is not accuracy.
slides.body: A useful agent should work across reruns, small changes, uncertainty, and bad outcomes.

slides.headline: Spends $8 to save $2?
slides.body: Princeton's point: accuracy and cost belong on the same chart.

slides.headline: Useful agents are boxed in.
slides.body: Narrow, checkable, reversible tasks are where agent workflows start to make sense.

slides.headline: Do not buy autonomy. Build supervision.
slides.body: Useful agents need logs, verifiers, permissions, tools, and human review.

slides.headline: Stop asking if agents are smart.
slides.body: Ask a better question: can this system fail safely when it is wrong?
slides.footer: Save this before the next demo
